newsitem.title: POLAND: Czech bourse leads E.European exchanges this week.
newsitem.headline: Czech bourse leads E.European exchanges this week.

text.p: The Prague bourse, buoyed by the right's strong showing in the first round of Senate elections, led other East European exchanges this week, with most markets seeing light trading volumes and subdued buying interest.
Warsaw shares inched up slightly amid a general sideways and the Budapest bourse rebounded on Friday.
The CESI Central European Share Index closed at 1,401.82 points on Friday, up 51.19 points or 3.70 percent.
PRAGUE

The Czech PX50 index posted five straight gains after a strong showing in the first round of Senate elections at the weekend gave a big lead to Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's right wing Civic Democratic Party (ODS).
Major issues led the way after a long run of losing sessions which had seen the PX50 lose 17 percent of its value since September 5.
Dealers were reluctant to predict a sustained bull run on the basis of one week's results and warned investors to wait for the second round of voting this coming weekend.
"This was just the first round and (the vote) isn't won yet," said Jan Sykora of Wood & Company in Prague.
In the week to Friday the top gainer among the blue chips was SPT Telecom, which rose 259 points, 9.4 percent, to 3,014.
WARSAW
Polish shares inched up for the second straight session on Friday and analysts saw another rise on Monday, saying the bourse had a chance to break out of its current sideways trend.
"The strong buying after price fixing of some large-cap, fundamentally sound stocks signals there could be significant demand," said Czeslaw Pospieszynski of Bank Gdanski brokerage.
The main market's all-share WIG index closed at 13,670.3 points on Friday, up 107.6 points or 0.8 percent from last Friday's close.
The week's biggest loser, insurer Polisa, fell 12.2 percent in the two sessions after opening 12.5 percent above issue.
Analysts said the firm looked fundamentally weak compared to the bourse's only other insurer, Warta, which eased two percent on the week.
BUDAPEST
The Budapest Stock Exchange closed the week in an upbeat mood as most leading shares on Friday saw significant gains and turnover doubled from Thursday.
Hungarian shares had fallen in profit-taking early in the week but then edged up, lifted by strong gains by Richter drug maker and oil and gas company MOL.

Traders attributed MOL's Friday rally to larger-than- expected energy price rises. The government announced on Thursday an 18.8 percent gas price rise for consumers effective from January 1, while the market expected around 16 percent.
One dealer said the market's optimism may be premature, as it was not clear what MOL's share from the price rise will be.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) saw another week of listless trade and the 12-share SAX index fell 16.32 points to 174.31 on Friday from Monday's opening at 190.63.
Brokers saw no revival in the near future.
BUCHAREST
Thin demand kept volumes light on the Bucharest bourse this week with buying interest centred on fertiliser maker Azomures SA and engineering company Artrom SA.
Two independent indices showed little movement with VAB slightly down and BIG just up over the week.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks ended the week mostly lower in lacklustre trade, and analysts said dullness would continue to plague the market with no major price changes in sight.

Some traders ascribed the stagnation to the unstable political situation. Croatia this week saw its first popular protests in years and President Franjo Tudjman has been treated in a Washington hospital for alleged stomach cancer.
But other analysts, citing the example of Zagrebacka Banka which traded well on Friday, said buyers were simply backing off as the Christmas season was approaching.
Total weekly stocks turnover fell to 30 million kuna from last week's 35.8 million.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell two percent this, with the SBI index down 23.2 points 1,152.2 points.
TIRANA
On Tirana's Stock Exchange 100 million leks ($980,400) worth of T-bills changed hands this week.
